The tool writes one formula per request. It works from the words you type. It does not open your spreadsheet, so the more exact your description, the better the formula.

**Keep the question to one result.** A request for a whole report needs several formulas. Ask for one result at a time, then build the next one from the first.

pages.h1: Excel formula generator for conditional formatting
pages.claim: Describe the cells you want to highlight, choose Excel or Google Sheets, and get the formula to paste into a conditional formatting rule. Free, no account, and the formula copies with one click.

sections.heading: How to get a conditional formatting formula
sections.body:
A conditional formatting rule colors a cell when a formula is true. The formula has to return TRUE or FALSE. You can write that formula yourself, or let the generator write it from a plain description.

Say three things in the box: the column that holds the test, the value that counts, and the cells you want colored. For example: highlight the name in column A when the status in column B says Overdue.

1. Open the [conditional formatting generator](https://excel-formula.lazur.app/conditional-formatting).
2. Choose Excel or Google Sheets in the app box.
3. Describe the cells, the test and the color in plain English.
4. Generate the formula and copy it.

sections.heading: Add the formula in Excel
sections.body:
Select the cells you want to color first. Then open the rule from the Home tab. Microsoft's guide for applying a formula in conditional formatting uses this path.

1. Select the cells, for example A2 to A100.
2. On the **Home** tab, click **Conditional Formatting**, then **New Rule**.
3. Choose the option **Use a formula to determine which cells to format**.
4. Paste the formula into the box. Write it for the first cell in your selection, here A2.
5. Click **Format**, set the fill or font color, then click **OK**.

Excel copies the rule to every other cell in the selection and moves the row reference for you. Read the full steps in [Microsoft's guide to using a formula for conditional formatting](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/excel/use-a-formula-to-apply-conditional-formatting-in-excel-for-mac).

sections.heading: Add the formula in Google Sheets
sections.body:
Google Sheets has the same idea, with a custom formula option in the side panel. Google's help page describes these steps.

1. Select the cells you want to format.
2. Click **Format**, then **Conditional formatting**. A panel opens on the right.
3. Under **Format cells if**, click **Custom formula is**.
4. Click the **Value or formula** box and paste the formula. It must start with an equals sign.
5. Pick the formatting style, then click **Done**.

As [Google's guide to conditional formatting](https://support.google.com/docs/answer/78413) explains, references are relative by default. Add dollar signs to lock a column or row that should not move.

sections.heading: Fix a rule that colors the wrong cells
sections.body:
Most rules that miss have one of three problems. Check them in this order.

- **The reference moves when it should not.** Put a dollar sign before the column letter, like $B2, so the test column stays fixed while the row changes.
- **The formula returns text, not TRUE or FALSE.** Conditional formatting needs the test to be TRUE or FALSE. Ask the generator for a test, not a result.
- **The formula looks at another sheet.** In Google Sheets, a custom formula can only use cells on the same sheet. Use the INDIRECT function to reach another sheet, or move the data onto the sheet.

An example for the rule above is =$B2="Overdue", applied to A2 to A100. Every row then checks its own status in column B and colors its own name in column A. Test it on three or four rows, and change the columns in the description if a row is wrong.

sections.heading: What a conditional formatting formula can do
sections.body:
A formula rule can test one cell, a whole row, or a value from another range. You can color a name when a date has passed, or shade a row when a box says Yes. You can also flag a repeat. For a repeat, a count formula such as COUNTIF over the column does the job.

Describe the test in words and say which cells should change color. If your request needs more than one rule, ask for one rule at a time and add each rule in the same way. Keep each description short, so the generator writes one clear formula.

faq.q: How do I create a formula for conditional formatting in Excel?
faq.a: Select the cells, then go to Home, Conditional Formatting, New Rule, and choose Use a formula to determine which cells to format. Paste a formula that returns TRUE or FALSE, written for the first cell in your selection, then set the format and click OK.

Yes. An AI tool can write an Excel formula from a plain description of the result you want. This generator writes one formula at a time for Excel or Google Sheets. Check the formula on a few rows with a known answer before you use it on the whole sheet.

faq.q: How do I create conditional formatting in Excel based on another cell?
faq.a: Write a formula that tests the other cell, starting with an equals sign. For example, =$B2="Overdue" colors a row when column B says Overdue. Use a dollar sign before the column so the test cell stays fixed while the rows change.
